top_evidence.document_title: Point-of-care testing for non-communicable diseases and health literacy outcomes: a systematic review
top_evidence.text: Meta-analysis was not feasible due to heterogeneity in intervention type (e.g. community screening vs. clinical monitoring), disease focus (e.g. diabetes, cardiovascular), outcome measurement tools (e.g. Patient Activation Measure, PAM-13; behaviour change), and population characteristics, which restricted comparability. We therefore employed a framework-guided narrative synthesis. Qualitative and quantitative outcome data were extracted and deductively coded against the five WHO health literacy actions ( Access , Understand , Appraise , Remember , Use ) to enable thematic comparison. Each outcome was mapped to the domains that best reflected the construct measured, and findings were then categorised by condition and type of POC test.

top_evidence.document_title: Point-of-care testing for non-communicable diseases and health literacy outcomes: a systematic review
top_evidence.text: Data extracted from each included study consisted of: authors, publication year, country, dates study was undertaken, cohort description, participant demographics (e.g. age, sex/gender, race), sample size, study design, data collection methods, exposure type (i.e. POC tests and measures), data analyses, and outcome data (i.e. health literacy measures). Health literacy measures could include direct assessment of health literacy, or indicators of health literacy via proxy measures such as patient activation, knowledge, motivation, adherence and behaviour change (validated or self-reported).

top_evidence.section: Risk Of Bias In Individual Studies
top_evidence.text: Risk of bias (quality) of individual studies was assessed using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT) [19]. The MMAT assessed included studies based on the study design; qualitative only, quantitative (non-randomised, randomised, descriptive), or mixed methods. Risk of bias was assessed by two independent researchers, with any discrepancies resolved through discussion or a third reviewer. Studies were not allocated a rating based on recommendations from the MMAT author [19].

top_evidence.document_title: Point-of-care testing for non-communicable diseases and health literacy outcomes: a systematic review
top_evidence.text: The review protocol was registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO; registration number CRD42022348011). A full protocol may be requested from the authors. Amendments to the original protocol included changes in author contributions, and health literacy outcomes were synthesised according to the World Health Organization (WHO) health literacy domains. The review was conducted and reported in line with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement (Additional file 1) [17].

top_evidence.document_title: Point-of-care testing for non-communicable diseases and health literacy outcomes: a systematic review
top_evidence.text: The database searches resulted in the identification of 12,459 records (Fig. 1). After removing duplicates, 6,129 unique records were retained for screening (Fig. 1). Title and abstract screening resulted in 98 records for further screening. Of these, 11 reports could not be retrieved (abstract-only, n = 7; non-written format, n = 2; inaccessible, n = 2), leaving 87 articles retained for full-text screening (Fig. 1). Thirteen articles were eligible for inclusion following the final screening stage (Fig. 1). This reduction highlights the limited availability of recent evidence investigating POC testing and health literacy outcomes.

top_evidence.document_title: Point-of-care testing for non-communicable diseases and health literacy outcomes: a systematic review
top_evidence.text: Eight studies met al.l quality criteria assessed by the MMAT [20-26, 28]. The MMAT assessment showed consistently clear research questions and appropriate data collection across most studies. However, two quantitative studies did not meet criteria for the interpretation of results based on the data provided [27, 29], while two did not account for confounders in analyses [31, 32]. One descriptive study failed to meet the criteria of low nonresponse bias [30]. All results from the risk of bias assessment can be seen in Additional file 3.
